stories.title: AI stock selloff spreads from Wall Street to South Korea's chip giants
stories.summary: U.S. stocks suffered their worst session since April 2025: the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, the Nasdaq 5.5%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 12.2%. Investors questioned AI infrastructure valuations and returns, while also weighing the possibility that political scrutiny and local opposition could slow data-centre construction. On Friday morning, South Korea's KOSPI fell 8.6% and triggered a 20-minute circuit breaker; Samsung fell 10% and SK Hynix 13%. The market moves are confirmed; the explanations are investor concerns, not proof that AI demand has collapsed or that new restrictions have been enacted.
stories.why: The AI build-out links chipmakers, cloud providers, power suppliers and data-centre construction across global markets. The selloff shows investors are repricing the cost, financing, policy and return-on-investment risks of that expansion.

stories.title: Ukraine reports 43 killed at aid site as airstrikes continue alongside peace talks
stories.summary: Russia and Ukraine exchanged drone and air attacks as two days of Brussels talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction, 2027 funding and security guarantees concluded. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 43 people had been confirmed dead after Russian guided bombs hit a school and shelter used as a humanitarian aid hub in Komyshuvakha; one previously missing person was found alive, while rescue teams continued searching. Russia said it targeted military units in the area. U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks are expected in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11; descriptions of the Brussels meetings as productive do not amount to a ceasefire agreement.
stories.why: The civilian toll and continuing attacks on infrastructure raise the stakes ahead of winter. The next round of talks could clarify security guarantees and reconstruction funding, but a diplomatic breakthrough remains uncertain.

stories.title: A wave of coding-agent deals puts developer workflow tools in the spotlight
stories.summary: Three developer-tool moves announced on November 4 point to consolidation around AI coding agents. OpenAI agreed to acquire Pierre, whose Trees and Diffs libraries already support file navigation and code review in Codex, and plans to bring Pierre's Git-based Code Storage features into Codex. Meta confirmed that Conductor is joining it; Conductor Cloud becomes read-only on November 13 and shuts down on November 20. Factory announced that HumanLayer is joining and says it will open-source HumanLayer. Financial terms were not disclosed; the OpenAI deal remains subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals.
stories.why: Competition is moving beyond model quality into the surrounding engineering workflow: parallel agents, Git history, code review and team collaboration. Developers should watch service-continuity dates and whether the open-source commitments are delivered.

stories.title: Grab agrees to cap combined fees and reimburse some drivers in Vietnam
stories.summary: Vietnam's competition commission says Grab has agreed to reduce some passenger and driver fees, cap its combined fees at no more than 32% of the amount paid by passengers, and reimburse about VND3.9 billion to drivers affected by excessive deductions. The watchdog said about 0.13% of trips since 2024 had deductions above 35%, partly due to algorithm errors or supply-and-demand fluctuations. Grab also plans VND912 billion in fourth-quarter driver incentives and operating-cost support, plus VND1.8 trillion in passenger promotions. Authorities say they will monitor implementation.
stories.why: The changes could improve fee transparency and driver take-home pay, but the practical effect depends on how the cap is calculated, whether reimbursements reach affected drivers and how consistently the watchdog enforces the commitments.

stories.title: Gas detected above Martian fissures hints that Alba Mons may not be fully dormant
stories.summary: The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride above fissures on the northern flank of Mars' Alba Mons volcano. Researchers say seasonal spikes are most consistent with volcanic seepage, possibly from a still-warm underground magma system; seasonal thawing may allow trapped gases to escape through ice-blocked fissures. This is evidence consistent with ongoing magmatic processes, not proof of a fresh eruption. Other chemical explanations remain possible, and the finding is not evidence of life.
stories.why: If confirmed, the result would change scientists' picture of Mars' internal heat and help identify subsurface environments that could be relevant to future habitability research. The potential hydrothermal-life connection remains speculative.
